title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
summary: Standardize how agent hosts discover and invoke external capabilities while keeping trust, authorization, and business policy explicit.
overview: MCP defines a protocol boundary between an application hosting an agent, its protocol clients, and servers exposing capabilities such as tools, resources, and prompts. It reduces custom integration plumbing; it does not make a server trustworthy or decide whether a proposed business action is authorized.

Treat discovery metadata and tool results as external input. The host still owns user intent, capability selection, approval policy, and result handling. Pin the supported protocol version and test the capabilities actually negotiated: a common envelope cannot guarantee identical semantics across independently implemented servers.

production.poc: A proof of concept may connect one trusted local server and inspect tool results manually; record which capabilities and transport assumptions it relies on.
production.production: Production requires server registration, schema validation, scoped credentials, operation timeouts, and explicit approval rules for mutating tools before enabling discovery broadly.
production.scale: Enterprise scale adds server ownership, version compatibility testing, per-tenant connection policy, capacity limits, and auditable capability changes across many teams.

components.name: Agent host
components.role: Owns user interaction, model context, tool policy, and approval boundaries.

components.name: Protocol client
components.role: Negotiates capabilities and manages the transport lifecycle for a server connection.

components.name: Registered MCP server
components.role: Exposes approved capabilities and validates incoming requests before calling downstream systems.

components.name: Authorization gateway
components.role: Enforces identity, audience, scope, resource access, and operation policy independently of model output.

components.name: Evidence and telemetry store
components.role: Records tool version, sanitized inputs, result status, and downstream operation identifiers.

flow.title: Select trusted connection
flow.description: Resolve the server from an administratively controlled registry with an owner and supported protocol version.

flow.title: Negotiate capabilities
flow.description: Initialize the connection and record available capabilities; reject unsupported requirements rather than assuming every server behaves identically.

flow.title: Bind authority
flow.description: Establish transport-appropriate credentials and downstream resource policy; never equate successful connection with permission for every tool.

flow.title: Validate invocation
flow.description: Check the chosen tool, argument schema, resource scope, deadline, and any required action approval before sending the request.

flow.title: Handle external output
flow.description: Validate result shape, preserve provenance, and treat returned text as evidence rather than new governing instructions.

flow.title: Reconcile effects
flow.description: For mutations, retain a stable operation identifier and query uncertain downstream outcomes before considering a retry.

useCase.title: Scoped support knowledge connector
useCase.situation: Illustrative architecture: A support assistant needs governed access to product documentation and customer case summaries through separately owned integrations.
useCase.problem: Custom adapters duplicate connection logic, but broad connector credentials would expose unrelated customer cases.
useCase.requirement: Provide interoperable discovery while enforcing customer assignment and read-only access for this workflow.
useCase.architecture: The host connects only to registered servers; a case service rechecks the authenticated support user's tenant and case scope.
useCase.failure: A server advertises a new write tool; host policy withholds it until the owner reviews its schema and action semantics.
useCase.impact: Measure integration maintenance effort, denied unauthorized requests, tool error rate, and evidence correctness; interoperability alone does not establish safety or quality.

tradeoffs.cost: Still requires server-specific semantic and security review.

tradeoffs.benefit: Allows integrations to evolve without hardcoding every tool.
tradeoffs.cost: Unexpected metadata changes need policy gates and compatibility checks.
Introduces network latency, identity management, and availability dependencies.

failures.scenario: A tool result contains instructions to disclose credentials.
failures.detection: Result handling detects an attempted action outside the authorized task and tool scope.
failures.recovery: Treat the text as untrusted evidence, block the action, and record the offending server response.

failures.scenario: A connection drops after a mutating downstream call.
failures.detection: The host has a submitted operation identifier but no confirmed result.
failures.recovery: Query the business system through a safe status path before retrying with the same logical operation key.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming protocol compliance implies trusted tools.
mistakes.fix: Review server ownership, downstream access, and mutation semantics separately.

mistakes.mistake: Passing one unrestricted credential through every server.
mistakes.fix: Use scoped, audience-bound credentials and enforce resource authorization at the service boundary.

mistakes.mistake: Letting tool descriptions override host instructions.
mistakes.fix: Keep discovery content in an untrusted data channel and apply host-owned capability policy.

whenToUse: Multiple agent hosts need a shared integration contract with independently maintained tools.
Connector teams can own versioning, authorization, and operational support for their servers.
A controlled capability registry can govern which tools each workflow may discover and invoke.
whenNotToUse: One fixed API call needs no discovery or shared connector ecosystem.
The proposed server cannot enforce resource access or provide a reliable ownership model.
Hard real-time control would depend on remote model-driven tool selection.
checklist: Pin and test the supported protocol version and negotiated capabilities.
Register each server owner, transport, trust boundary, and incident contact.
Validate tool schemas and mutation semantics before exposing them to models.
Enforce user, tenant, audience, and resource scope at every protected boundary.
Define timeouts and reconciliation for ambiguous mutating calls.
Treat tool metadata and results as untrusted external content.
Test server changes against denied-action and compatibility scenarios.
